Just now

--

On a lazy afternoon, sipping a sweet paper cup of Maxim instant coffee, I stare at some old C code. Floating above the lines on the screen are familiar stars (asterisks).
To the modern developers who started coding in an era where garbage collectors quietly sweep up the mess and everything is safely wrapped in something called a ‘reference’, this star might look like a strange relic. The pointer. It is not about politely accepting data handed to you; it is about grabbing the 16-bit hex address where the data sleeps and picking the lock yourself. It is a powerful key, but one wrong turn brings the entire program crashing down with a Segmentation Fault. And when handling this dangerous key, a very old and stubborn holy war wages among C programmers.
It starts with a simple question: Where exactly should this star be placed?
int* p;
// or
int *p;The ‘Type’ faction pulls the star right up against the type: int* p;. It is a declaration: "The essence of this variable is not a simple integer, but an integer pointer." It is philosophically elegant and intuitive.
On the other hand, the 'Variable' faction places the star right in front of the variable name: int *p;. This approach, chosen by the creators of C (K&R), is fiercely behavioral. *"If you follow p (p), you will find an integer (int) waiting for you."
Years ago, when I was writing a book on data structures and algorithms in C, I had a real headache navigating the massive rift between these two camps. In my heart, I supported the elegance of the Type faction. But every time I typed the following code only to watch the compiler coldly betray me—turning p into a pointer while downgrading q into a mere integer—I had to stop typing and grab the back of my neck in frustration.
int* p, q;During my days working at a telecom equipment company, I came across a bizarre compromise while reviewing legacy code.
int * p;A single space of distance from both the type and the variable. When I first saw this bizarre neutral zone, I had to hold my breath for a second. While the two major factions were fighting tooth and nail, were the people who left this star floating in zero gravity pacifists, or just apathetic engineers who had turned it into space debris?
“The code isn’t product, the system is.”
A phrase I often chew on suddenly crossed my mind. Right. This spacing wasn’t a compromise. It was cold pragmatism relying on the mechanical truth that the compiler simply ignores whitespace and parses it anyway. It was a statement of cold nihilism toward the system, implying that human cognitive structures and philosophical debates mean absolutely nothing in front of the machine.
Exhausted by this endless debate over the star’s orbit, some senior programmers eventually decided to just hide the star out of sight altogether. This happened in the barbaric era before typedef had properly settled in, when people treated the preprocessor like a Swiss Army knife, heavily abusing #define macros.
They tried to use this text replacer to forge the pointer into one perfect, unified type.
#define INTPTR int*How clean. But when the aforementioned INTPTR p, q; disaster inevitably struck again, some realized the limits of the preprocessor and resorted to the extreme measure of tearing the star off the macro entirely.
#define MY_INT int
MY_INT *p, *q;But this meant the complete failure of abstraction. The grand dream of elevating the pointer to a clean, independent type was shattered. The detached star didn’t disappear into thin air; it came back like a boomerang to stick right back onto the programmer’s fingers. “You skip struggle, you skip engineering.” The price for trying to dodge complexity by hiding behind a cheap trick was steep. They essentially surrendered to the Variable faction.
To make matters worse, leaving the star in the macro created a total disaster when tangled with const.
#define INTPTR int*
const INTPTR p;
// Expands to: const int* p (A pointer to a constant integer)But if you use the later-introduced typedef, the philosophical meaning of what we were trying to keep immutable completely flips.
